0.title: Opening Our Lives and Our Homes
0.essay:
We live in an age of many connections and few friends. People have hundreds of online contacts, yet often no one they could call at two in the morning.

A lonely age

Loneliness has become widespread. It affects the young and the old, the single and the married. At the same time, homes have become private retreats, and the old habit of having people round for a meal has faded in many places. We are more connected and more isolated than ever.

What Scripture offers

The Bible has a great deal to say about both friendship and hospitality. God made us for relationship. Jesus called his disciples friends. The early church met in homes and broke bread together. And hospitality, which in the New Testament literally means “love of strangers,” is a command for every Christian, not just a gift for a few.

The chapters

This study looks at why we were made for friendship, what makes a true friend, how to choose friends wisely, why hospitality matters, and how God’s welcome to us shapes our welcome to others: Made for Friendship; Marks of a True Friend; Choosing Friends Wisely; The Ministry of Hospitality; and Welcomed by God, Welcoming Others.

For reflection

Who would you call at two in the morning if you were in trouble? And who would call you?

1.title: Made for Friendship
1.essay:
In a world God called good, one thing was not good. “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). We were made for one another.

Not good to be alone

God’s first answer to Adam’s loneliness was marriage, but the principle reaches wider. Human beings were made for relationship. That is no accident. We reflect a God who is himself a fellowship of love: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Before the world began, God was never alone. To be made in his image is to be made for communion.

Two are better than one

The Preacher in Ecclesiastes describes a lonely man who works endlessly with no one to share it with. Then he praises companionship: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Friends help us in our work. They lift us when we fall, warm us when we are cold, and stand with us when we are attacked. And he adds, “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Life is meant to be shared.

Quality, not quantity

Proverbs makes an important distinction: “A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). Many acquaintances are not the same as true friends. A crowd of shallow connections can melt away when trouble comes. One loyal friend is worth more.

Jesus calls us friends

On the night before his death, Jesus said something astonishing to his disciples: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). The Lord of glory calls his followers friends. He shares his heart with them.

And he showed the greatest friendship of all. “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Within hours he would do exactly that. Friendship with Jesus is the foundation of all Christian friendship.

Friends of God

Abraham “was called a friend of God” (James 2:23). Of Moses we read that the LORD spoke with him “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). This comes in the middle of a story of Israel’s rebellion, a sudden picture of closeness. Through Christ, every believer is brought into this friendship with God. It is the deepest friendship there is, and it shapes all the others.

Friendship in the church

The church is a family of brothers and sisters, and deep friendships should grow within it. But friendship is particular. We cannot be close friends with everyone. Even Jesus, who loved all his disciples, had an inner circle of three, Peter, James and John, and one who is called “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” It is not unloving to have special friends. It is human.

Friendship and marriage

Marriage at its best includes deep friendship. The bride in the Song of Songs says of her husband, “This is my beloved and this is my friend” (Song of Solomon 5:16). Yet married people also need other friends. No spouse can meet every relational need, and it is unfair to expect one to.

Across the generations

Scripture values friendships between older and younger believers: Naomi and Ruth, Elijah and Elisha, Paul and Timothy. Such friendships pass on wisdom and faith. A church where the generations never mix misses one of its richest gifts.

Even Paul needed friends

In his final letter, written from prison, Paul mentions many friends by name. He asks Timothy to come quickly and to bring Mark, and his cloak. He writes, “Luke alone is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). The great apostle needed friends, and he was not ashamed to say so.

Think of a man in his fifties who realises that, apart from his wife, he has no close friends. His life has been work and family. He asks two men from church to meet for breakfast once a month. At first it feels awkward. Five years later, they are the first people he calls in a crisis.

For reflection

Who are your closest friends, and how did those friendships begin? Is there someone in your church who seems lonely, and how could you reach out to them?

2.title: Marks of a True Friend
2.essay:
Scripture paints a clear picture of what true friendship looks like. Its marks are loyalty, honesty, counsel, presence and forgiveness, and every one of them is found perfectly in Christ.

Loyalty

“A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Proverbs 17:17). True friends stay in hard times. When Naomi was bereaved and bitter, and urged her daughter-in-law to go home, Ruth refused to leave her: “For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16). Ruth bound herself to Naomi’s people, Naomi’s God and even Naomi’s grave. Her loyalty became faith, as she joined the people of the LORD.

Covenant love

The friendship of David and Jonathan is one of the most moving in Scripture. “The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:1). Jonathan made a covenant with David and gave him his own robe, armour, sword, bow and belt.

Think what that meant. Jonathan was the king’s son and heir, yet he handed David the symbols of his own position. He defended David before his father and risked his life to protect him. He rejoiced in David’s future, even though it meant he would never be king. True friendship is generous and humble.

When they parted for the last time, with Saul hunting David, “they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most” (1 Samuel 20:41). When Jonathan later died in battle, David lamented, “very pleasant have you been to me” (2 Samuel 1:26).

Honesty

“Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6). A true friend tells us the truth, even when it hurts. Flatterers tell us what we want to hear. Friends tell us what we need to hear. Proverbs adds, “Better is open rebuke than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5). A friend who never risks saying anything hard is not much of a friend.

Counsel and sharpening

“Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel” (Proverbs 27:9). Friends help us think, decide and see what we cannot see alone. And they make us better: “Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17). Good friends challenge, encourage and stretch one another in faith and character.

Proverbs also says, “Do not forsake your friend and your father’s friend” (Proverbs 27:10). Long-standing friendships, even across the generations, are precious.

Presence in suffering

When Job lost everything, his three friends came to comfort him. They wept and tore their robes, and then “they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great” (Job 2:13). Their silence was their best ministry. They went wrong only later, when they started explaining his suffering. Sometimes the best thing a friend can do is simply be there.

Forgiveness

“Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates close friends” (Proverbs 17:9). No friendship lasts long without overlooking small offences and forgiving larger ones. Friends who keep score do not stay friends.

Christ the true friend

Every mark of friendship is found perfectly in Christ. He is loyal: he never leaves us. He is honest: he tells us the truth about ourselves. He is wise in counsel, present in suffering and quick to forgive. And he laid down his life for his friends. Christian friendship is a reflection of his.

Friendship costs

Real friendship costs time, effort, inconvenience and sometimes reputation. Jonathan risked his father’s anger. Ruth gave up her homeland. True friends give themselves.

Friends of the same sex

Deep friendships between men, and between women, are good and biblical. Our culture often sexualises close friendships or regards them with suspicion. Scripture honours them.

Think of two women who became friends at a church toddler group twenty years ago. Since then they have walked together through a divorce, a cancer diagnosis, rebellious teenagers and the death of parents. They have also told each other hard truths. Each says the other is God’s gift to her.

For reflection

Which of these marks of friendship are you strongest in, and which do you most need to grow in? How could you be a better friend to someone this month?

3.title: Choosing Friends Wisely
3.essay:
Friends shape us more than we realise. Over time we absorb the values, habits and attitudes of those we spend time with. That is why Scripture urges wisdom in choosing them.

We become like our friends

“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (Proverbs 13:20). This simple proverb states a powerful principle. We cannot avoid being shaped by those around us, so we must choose carefully. Paul quotes a saying well known in his day: “Bad company ruins good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Some company is dangerous

Proverbs gives specific warnings. “Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare” (Proverbs 22:24–25). The reason is not that such people are beyond love. It is that their ways are contagious. We may learn their habits without noticing.

Gossip is the same: “A dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends” (Proverbs 16:28). Some friendships call for caution.

Walking, standing, sitting

The Psalms open with a portrait of the blessed person: “Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers” (Psalm 1:1). Notice the progression: walking, then standing, then sitting. Influence usually grows gradually. We drift alongside, then linger, then settle. Instead, the blessed person delights in God’s law and is like a tree planted by streams of water. Our companions and our meditations together shape who we become.

Friends with unbelievers

None of this means Christians should have no unbelieving friends. Jesus was mocked as “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19), and he wore the name gladly. Christians should love, befriend and serve those who do not yet believe. We are called to be salt and light, and salt does nothing if it stays in the jar.

But salt must not lose its saltiness. Jesus befriended sinners without becoming like them. His holiness was not threatened by their company. Rather, they were changed by his. That is the model. Our closest friends, the ones who shape our decisions and values, should share our faith. A good question to ask of any friendship is simply this: who is influencing whom?

Choosing advisers

When Solomon’s son Rehoboam became king, he faced his first big decision. The older men who had served his father advised him to listen to the people. But he “abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him” (1 Kings 12:8). His friends gave him foolish advice, and he lost most of his kingdom. The friends we listen to matter.

Think of a teenager who starts spending time with a new group who mock church and drink heavily. Over a few months his parents notice his attitude changing. A youth leader befriends him, invites him to a Christian camp and helps him find friends who share his faith. His other friendships continue, but they no longer shape him most.

Be the friend you seek

Choosing friends wisely is not only about finding good people. It is about becoming one. Rather than only looking for good friends, aim to be a good friend: loyal, honest, encouraging and godly. Often the friend we long for is the friend we have never quite been.

When friendships fail

Even good friendships can be broken by sin, misunderstanding or distance. David’s trusted counsellor Ahithophel betrayed him and joined Absalom’s rebellion. David poured out his pain: “For it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it” (Psalm 55:12). The wound was that it came from “my companion, my familiar friend” (Psalm 55:13), one with whom he had walked to God’s house.

Jesus himself was betrayed by Judas, one of the twelve. Betrayal by a friend is one of the deepest wounds there is. Where possible, seek reconciliation. Where not, do as David did and bring it to God, who never betrays.

For reflection

Who are the three people who influence you most? Are they leading you towards Christ or away from him? And what kind of friend are you to them?

4.title: The Ministry of Hospitality
4.essay:
Hospitality is not a hobby for people with large homes and a gift for cooking. It is a command for every Christian, and one of the most powerful ways of showing the love of Christ.

A command for all

Paul writes, “Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality” (Romans 12:13). The word seek suggests active pursuit, not waiting for opportunities to arrive. Peter adds, “Show hospitality to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4:9). And it is a requirement for church leaders (1 Timothy 3:2). Hospitality is not optional.

Love of strangers

The New Testament word for hospitality combines “love” and “stranger.” It means welcoming not only friends but those outside our usual circle. “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2).

This recalls Abraham. Sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day, he saw three travellers. He ran to meet them, bowed, and hurried to prepare a meal (Genesis 18:1–8). He may not have known at first that the LORD himself was among them. We never know whom God is sending to our door.

Not for repayment

Jesus once told a host, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you” (Luke 14:12–14).

Christian hospitality is not social networking. It reaches those who cannot return the favour. It reflects the kingdom, where the least are honoured guests at God’s table, and Jesus says the reward will come “at the resurrection of the just” (Luke 14:14).

Without grumbling

Peter’s phrase is realistic. Hospitality can be inconvenient, tiring and costly. Guests can be difficult. Children can be noisy. But we are to open our homes cheerfully, as an act of love. Peter places it between love and spiritual gifts: love covers many sins, hospitality should be shown without grumbling, and gifts should be used to serve one another (1 Peter 4:8–11). Hospitality is a practical way of stewarding God’s grace.

Simple is fine

Hospitality does not require a perfect house or an elaborate meal. It means opening our lives: a cup of tea, soup and bread, a seat at the family table. The point is welcome, not impressing guests. Many people never invite anyone because they feel their home or cooking is not good enough. But guests rarely remember the food. They remember being wanted.

The early church

The first Christians broke bread in their homes and “received their food with glad and generous hearts” (Acts 2:46). Homes were the centres of Christian community and mission. Lydia opened her home to Paul and his companions (Acts 16:15). Priscilla and Aquila hosted a church in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19).

In the Old Testament, a wealthy woman in Shunem noticed the prophet Elisha passing through. She said to her husband, “Let us make a small room on the roof with walls and put there for him a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp” (2 Kings 4:10). Her simple, thoughtful hospitality led to God’s blessing on her family.

Hospitality and mission

Many people who would never come to a church will come to a home for a meal. Hospitality is one of the most natural and effective ways of sharing life and faith with neighbours who do not believe. Conversations happen around a table that would never happen in a pew.

Think of a busy family who decide to keep one Sunday lunch a month for inviting people from church they do not know well: newcomers, international students, those living alone. The food is simple and the house is often messy. Over the years, dozens of people tell them those lunches made them feel they belonged.

Wisdom and safety

Hospitality should be practised with wisdom. Families should think about the safety of their children, and churches should help members discern when and how to welcome people they do not know. Love is not naive.

For reflection

When did you last have someone in your home who could not repay you? What keeps you from practising hospitality more, and what one act of welcome could you plan for the coming month?

5.title: Welcomed by God, Welcoming Others
5.essay:
The deepest reason for Christian hospitality is not that it is useful or kind. It is that God has welcomed us.

Christ has welcomed you

Paul writes, “Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). We were strangers and enemies, outside the household of God. But in Christ we have been brought near. “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). God has invited us to his table. Christ’s welcome is both the pattern and the motive for ours, and the goal is the glory of God.

Paul gave this command to a church divided between Jewish and Gentile believers, who disagreed about food and holy days. Welcoming across cultural, social and generational lines is a powerful sign of the gospel’s reconciling power.

Jesus welcomed sinners

The religious leaders complained about Jesus: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). They meant it as an insult. It is one of the most beautiful things ever said about him. Jesus ate with tax collectors, fed thousands on a hillside and welcomed the outcast to his table.

Zacchaeus was rich and despised, a tax collector who had grown wealthy by cheating his own people. Jesus saw him in a tree and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today” (Luke 19:5). The crowd grumbled. But Zacchaeus received Jesus joyfully, gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated. Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9), “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). His welcome changed a life.

Welcoming the foreigner

In the Old Testament, God commanded Israel to welcome the sojourner: “You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34). Israel’s own history of being foreigners was to make them merciful.

Christians, once spiritual strangers ourselves, should likewise show kindness to those far from home. Think of a church in a city with many international students that starts a Friday evening meal in members’ homes. Students come from many countries, some far from family for the first time. Over the years friendships form, Bible studies begin, and several students come to faith. Others return home with warm memories of Christians who welcomed them.

Serving Christ in his people

Jesus said that on the last day the King will say, “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35). The righteous will ask when they ever did this, and he will answer, “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

Some read “the least of these my brothers” as referring to all poor people. But elsewhere in Matthew, Jesus’ brothers are his disciples (Matthew 12:49–50; 28:10). So the passage most naturally speaks of how the world treats Christ’s needy followers. Jesus identifies so closely with them that welcoming them is welcoming him. At the same time, the Bible’s wider teaching, as in the parable of the Good Samaritan, calls Christians to show mercy to every neighbour in need.

Not earning a welcome

Welcoming others does not earn God’s welcome. It flows from it. We do not open our homes in order to be accepted by God. We open them because we already have been. Those who have been welcomed become welcoming.

The great banquet

All hospitality now points forward to the feast to come. “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). Every meal shared in Christ’s name is a small foretaste of that table, where people from every nation will sit together with the Lord who welcomed them. A pot of soup and a few chairs around a kitchen table can be a preview of heaven.

For reflection

How has Christ welcomed you? Who in your community is a stranger, far from home or on the margins, and how could you welcome them as he welcomed you?
